item.content:encoded:
Ubuntu Summit 26.10: Less than a week away!

Here in London, the long summer has stepped aside for cooler nights and damp, misty mornings. The trees are turning amber and the sunlight is low on the horizon, which can only mean one thing: the next Ubuntu Summit is just around the corner. In fact, it’s next week, Thursday and Friday, November 12-13.

This will be our third Summit since switching to our twice-yearly schedule. What initially seemed like a huge challenge, fitting a year of planning into six months, then starting again, has become a massive opportunity for those of us who put the event together.

Much like the release early, release often software development philosophy (which many of our teams have adopted here at Canonical), frequency forces you to get good at what’s important. And what’s most important at a remote-first event like the Ubuntu Summit is the quality of the talks and presentations. With a fresh Summit every six months, we’re able to capture the best of what’s happening now and present the freshest ideas to the community. Never has moving fast been more important.

And because we are broadcasting a live, interactive stream from our base in London, you get to experience this immediately, whether you are watching at home or joining one of the local watch parties. You can ask questions to our speakers, take part in interactive activities, and poke around the latest open source developments without having to book a flight.

When you gather this often, conversations shift from distant, theoretical roadmaps to what people are actually designing, developing and deploying today. Our Ubuntu Summit 26.10 Timetable reflects this, which you can see from just the first morning’s sessions:

  • Astra: an open-source observatory control software for exoplanet hunting: The development and application of open-source software used in astronomical observatories to detect and track exoplanets.
  • ntfy: the joys of handling 4 million push notifications per day: An architectural overview of scaling backend infrastructure and managing high-throughput message delivery.
  • hax: AI coding agent as a lightweight Unix tool: How to integrate large language models into traditional, terminal-based developer workflows using established Unix principles.
  • How local AI is transforming Ubuntu accessibility: Our big news for Ubuntu – the integration of locally processed artificial intelligence models to improve user accessibility features within the desktop environment.
  • Text to CAD: how I designed a robot with LLMs and open source tools: The practical application of open-source software and large language models in physical engineering and robotics design.

Register today (it’s free!) and we’ll see you next week.

item.content:encoded:
We recently announced the launch of Zephyr 26.04 LTS, bringing up to 15 years of security maintenance per LTS and enterprise lifecycle management to microcontroller-grade devices.

While central high-performance computer ECUs capture most of the industry spotlight in software-defined vehicle (SDV) architectures, the operational reality of modern vehicles is far more distributed. Under the chassis sit hundreds of microcontroller-based electronic control units (ECUs) managing real-time sensor loops, power distribution, and domain specific control tasks.

These lightweight microcontrollers (MCUs) present a huge cybersecurity vulnerability if left unmanaged over multi-decade vehicle lifecycles. With Zephyr LTS, those same MCUs now receive long-term support, expanding support across the entire software-defined vehicle (SDV) architecture.

The compliance gap

Traditional MCU lifecycle management relies on custom downstream open-source forks or proprietary RTOS distributions. This creates an unsustainable, fragmented engineering burden:

Engineering silos: In-house teams spend thousands of hours applying security patches to legacy RTOS forks rather than building new product developments.

Supply chain vulnerabilities: Unpatched microcontrollers can become backdoors into primary vehicle buses like CAN or Ethernet AVB.

Compliance bottlenecks: Tracking SBOM across dozens of disparate vendor toolchains and SDKs slows regulatory audits and increases liability risks under ISO/SAE 21434.

Turnkey compliance and enterprise lifecycle support

Maintaining cybersecurity across a decade-long vehicle deployment demands a stable, predictable foundation. Zephyr 26.04 LTS addresses technical debt and regulatory mandates through key capabilities:

  • Up to 15 years of support per LTS: Canonical provides CVE monitoring, security patching, and SBOM generation for up to 15 years. This removes long-term compliance friction for automotive fleets.
  • Predictable release cadence: Zephyr LTS mirrors Ubuntu’s established release cycle, delivering LTS releases every two years and interim updates every six months to provide dependable roadmap predictability.
  • Full stack tooling coverage: We maintain the core Zephyr’s RTOS kernel alongside essential build tools like West (Zephyr’s meta-tool for building, flashing, and managing repositories).

Development agility with Canonical Workshop

Decoupling hardware from software requires frictionless developer tooling and reliable remote deployment mechanisms. To accelerate time-to-market and streamline onboarding across distributed teams, Zephyr LTS integrates Canonical Workshop.

Canonical Workshop is an open-source tool developed by Canonical that launches sandboxed, reproducible development environments on Ubuntu using a single command.  Using the Workshop SDK for Zephyr 26.04 LTS, developers can access a ready-to-use Zephyr LTS environment on any hardware, complete with essential build tools. This allows engineering teams to bypass complex local toolchain configurations and execute tools like West immediately.

Zephyr LTS delivers the deterministic real time performance for your critical tasks, andCanonical manages the long-term security, compliance and patches –enabling your developers to ship features rapidly.

Get in touch with our automotive experts

Navigating multi-decade security maintenance and regulatory compliance does not have to slow down your engineering teams. Whether you are architecting next-generation SDVs or looking to secure MCU-class ECUs, our team is here to help.

Contact our automotive team today to discuss your architecture requirements, request a demonstration, or explore how Zephyr LTS fits into your production roadmap.

item.title: Ubuntu Pro is now available on AWS Deep Learning Amazon Machine Images (DLAMI)
item.description: In September 2026, Amazon Web Services (AWS) published its first DLAMIs built on Ubuntu Pro in the Base GPU family. By choosing Ubuntu Pro, enterprises launching DLAMIs gain a stronger security maintenance posture at launch thanks to Expanded Security Maintenance (ESM). What are the DLAMIs? The DLAMIs are AWS-maintained machine images for GPU and accelerator […]
item.content:encoded:
In September 2026, Amazon Web Services (AWS) published its first DLAMIs built on Ubuntu Pro in the Base GPU family. By choosing Ubuntu Pro, enterprises launching DLAMIs gain a stronger security maintenance posture at launch thanks to Expanded Security Maintenance (ESM).

What are the DLAMIs?

The DLAMIs are AWS-maintained machine images for GPU and accelerator instances. Each ships the NVIDIA driver, CUDA, the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking stack, and the surrounding tooling already installed and tested together. This means a GPU node is productive on first boot, rather than after a day of driver work. 

These images cover 31 actively built lines: Base AMIs carrying the drivers alone, framework images with PyTorch preinstalled, and Neuron images for Trainium and Inferentia. 

What is included in Ubuntu Pro DLAMI images?

Ubuntu Pro DLAMI is available as a base GPU image for typical AI workloads on the latest GPU hardware. There are four versions of the image split across 2 Ubuntu releases and 2 architectures. This enables a broad support of instance types, including Grace Blackwell architecture. It ships with NVIDIA driver 595.91.07 and several CUDA toolkits.

The x86 images cover 14 GPU families, from G4dn and G5 through P4d, P5, and P5en, to the Blackwell P6-B200 and P6-B300. The ARM images cover G5g and the Grace Blackwell P6e-GB200 and P6e-GB300 instance families.

Enterprise grade images with Ubuntu Pro

GPU images have been preconfigured with a pinned kernel for stability and compatibility purposes. The NVIDIA and EFA drivers are compiled against it, so AWS holds the kernel packages and ships security fixes as a new image every week or two. 

Ubuntu Pro comes with ESM by default, which expands security updates from the Main repository (the primary Ubuntu repository, maintained by Canonical’s engineers) to Universe (the community-maintained repository of Ubuntu) and extends the overall security coverage from 5 to 10 years. This solves a major compliance challenge for enterprises that cannot rely solely on community support. The Universe repository contains many key AI/ML dependencies, which the default DLAMI already has included at launch. 

It also enables Kernel Livepatch, delivering in-memory security updates for the active kernel to prevent unexpected reboots. This is especially important for GPU accelerated machines, which are typically dedicated to continuous, long-running operations.

Supporting NVIDIA Grace Blackwell P6e-GB200 and P6e-GB300 instance types

For the first time on AWS, Ubuntu Pro DLAMIs provide out-of-the-box NVIDIA Grace Blackwell support across its two variants: GB200 and GB300.  While Ubuntu Pro 24.04 LTS supports both P6e-GB200 and P6e-GB300, Ubuntu Pro 22.04 LTS supports only P6e-GB200. 

Kernel livepatch on ARM64 is available from Ubuntu 26.04 LTS onwards.

What ESM covers on the image

If you’re curious to know whether the Ubuntu Pro variant is for you, you can either run pro security-status --esm-apps on the Ubuntu Pro 24.04 LTS Base GPU image, or continue reading.

The Ubuntu Pro DLAMI base image comes with 38 pre-installed packages from the Universe repository. These packages are covered by Ubuntu Pro from launch, and include key packages commonly used on AI workloads at scale:

However, these packages are only the starting point. With every deployment built, more packages and dependencies will be drawn in, the majority of which often come from the Universe repository. These packages receive support only through a Canonical Pro subscription, through ESM. 

How to get the images

Each image line has a public AWS Systems Manager (SSM) parameter that resolves to its latest build. You can get the images by running the following commands with AWS CLI.

For AMD64 images:

aws ssm get-parameters --names /aws/service/deeplearning/ami/x86_64/base-oss-nvidia-driver-gpu-ubuntu-pro-24.04/latest/ami-id
aws ssm get-parameters --names /aws/service/deeplearning/ami/arm64/base-oss-nvidia-driver-gpu-ubuntu-pro-24.04/latest/ami-id

For ARM64 (Graviton and NVIDIA Grace Blackwell):

aws ssm get-parameters --names /aws/service/deeplearning/ami/arm64/base-oss-nvidia-driver-gpu-ubuntu-pro-24.04/latest/ami-id

If you want to check whether your Ubuntu Pro subscription is active, run pro status on a live instance to see your active entitlements and configurations.

Conclusion and Next Steps

Bringing Ubuntu Pro to the AWS DLAMIs provides enterprises with an ESM posture right out of the box. With Canonical’s commitment to support and maintain Universe packages for 10 years, and Kernel Livepatch enabling seamless patching without reboots, organizations can confidently run AI workloads while meeting stringent security and compliance standards.

Ready to enhance your GPU workloads? Get started today by launching the new Ubuntu Pro DLAMIs on AMD64 images or ARM64, or visit the AWS Deep Learning AMI Documentation for detailed setup guides and deployment options. If you have any questions, contact us here.

item.title: CVE-2026-109518 APT vulnerability fixes available
item.description: Fixes are available in Ubuntu for the CVE-2026-109518 vulnerability affecting APT.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Max Justicz discovered and responsibly disclosed a vulnerability in APT, the package manager used in Debian, Ubuntu, and derivative Linux distributions. The vulnerability has been assigned the identifier CVE-2026-109518 and has a severity of High. An on-path attacker who can manipulate the HTTP traffic between a system and an archive server can trigger the installation of an attacker-controlled .deb package file and obtain root privileges on the target system. We have released security updates for all affected Ubuntu releases. Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish) and newer releases are affected by default; older releases are only affected if the Acquire::Retries APT configuration setting is set to a non-zero value.

The vulnerability has a CVSS 4.0 score of 7.7, corresponding to a severity of High (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N).

The vulnerability exists in the HTTP backend invoked by the APT library, and affects any APT-based frontend (apt, apt-get, aptitude, or any of the Ubuntu graphical applications).

The vulnerability does not affect software installation via snap packages, as snaps use a different package management system.

The use of TLS via HTTPS protects against this vulnerability, as exploitation requires the attacker to manipulate HTTP traffic. This post describes how to enable HTTPS for APT traffic. Other transport methods (such as FTP) are not affected by this vulnerability.

The vulnerability requires the client to retry a failed download. This is controlled by the Acquire::Retries APT configuration setting. If this is set to 0, no downloads are retried and the vulnerability cannot be exploited. This configuration setting is only set to a non-zero value in Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish) and newer releases.

Which Ubuntu releases are affected by CVE-2026-109518?

How to check if you are impacted by CVE-2026-109518

Compare the version of the installed packages from the APT source with the versions in the table above.

apt list --installed '?source-package(^apt$)'

Impact of CVE-2026-109518

An attacker can exploit the vulnerability only if the target system attempts to install a .deb package. An on-path attacker that can manipulate the HTTP traffic between the APT client and the archive server used can replace one of the package files retrieved with an-attacker controlled one. Normally, the archive signature scheme protects against this kind of attack. However, the vulnerability allows an attacker to trick APT into installing a package even if it fails signature verification.

When the system installs a .deb package, it executes the package’s scripts with root privileges. Therefore, the installation of untrusted packages is strongly discouraged as it leads to system compromise. This vector can be used by an attacker who can exploit the vulnerability to achieve root privileges on the target system.

A malicious package mirror can similarly exploit the vulnerability to deliver unsigned, malicious packages to target systems. The archive signature scheme normally secures package mirrors; therefore, once users update the APT client library on the end-user system, compromised mirrors no longer pose a risk.”

Enabling TLS

If you have concerns about the network path to the selected Ubuntu archive server, you can enable TLS as a mitigating measure. Once this vulnerability is patched, enabling TLS is only necessary as a future precaution. The archive signature scheme remains a much stronger integrity protection safeguard that provides end-to-end verification, not just during transit (as TLS does).

However, where the possibility of an on-path attacker cannot be eliminated, enabling TLS prior to installing the security updates for this vulnerability ensures there is no point in which an attacker could exploit the vulnerability.

To enable TLS, modify the APT sources configured and replace http:// URLs with https:// ones. The APT sources files are in /etc/apt/sources.list and the /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ drop-in directory, using either the DEB22 format in .sources files or the older line-oriented format in .list files.

You can replace all HTTP URLs pointing to the Ubuntu archive to HTTPs ones with the following command:

sudo sed -Ei 's!http://((([a-z]+\.)?archive|security|ports)\.ubuntu\.com)!https://\1!' /etc/apt/sources.list /etc/apt/sources.list.d/*.list /etc/apt/sources.list.d/*.sources

Please note that the command does not modify URLs which may point to other mirrors or package repositories. You should then update the local package list and ensure that no errors occur (which could happen if a package mirror does not support HTTPS):

sudo apt update

Please note that some mirrors operated by the community, including some country-specific mirrors, do not support HTTPS. 

While enabling TLS provides protection against this particular vulnerability when exploited by an on-path attacker, we strongly recommend that you install the security updates, as described in the following section.

How to apply fixes for CVE-2026-109518

Temporarily setting Acquire::Retries to zero while installing this security update provides a mitigation against this vulnerability, whether exploited by an on-path attacker or a potentially malicious mirror.

We recommend you upgrade all packages:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -o Acquire::Retries=0

If this is not possible, the affected component can be targeted:

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -o Acquire::Retries=0 --only-upgrade '?source-package(^apt$)'

The unattended-upgrades feature is enabled by default for Ubuntu 16.04 LTS onwards. This service:  

  • Applies new security updates every 24 hours automatically.
  • If you have this enabled, the patches above will be automatically applied within 24 hours of being available.

Ubuntu 26.10, 26.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, and 22.04 LTS receive these fixes as part of standard support. If you are using Ubuntu 20.04 LTS or older, the Ubuntu Pro subscription offers coverage for up to 15 years. Ubuntu 20.04 LTS and 18.04 LTS are covered by Expanded Security Maintenance (ESM), while Ubuntu 16.04 LTS and 14.04 LTS require ESM with the Legacy add-on. Ubuntu Pro is free for up to 5 machines, or up to 50 machines for community members. Ubuntu Pro also provides access to Landscape which enables you to control the roll-out of security fixes across your estate. Learn more.

If you work with robots, perhaps you’ve come up against a common, but annoying situation: the one field run that mattered is the one nobody recorded. Or it was recorded but the ROS 2 bag (a recording of ROS 2 topics) is sitting in the robot’s storage, at a customer site, three time zones away.

This issue is commonly caused by manually starting ros2 bag record and using scp to copy gigabytes off the robot after every test, which just does not scale. It can also lead to missing bag synchronizations or accidental overwrites.

There is a better way: let every robot record itself continuously and upload its bags to your server automatically. That is exactly what the ros2-exporter-agent snap does.

What can the ros2-exporter-agent do?

The snap runs four small cooperating services on the robot:

  • recorder: records your ROS 2 topics to MCAP bags, splitting them by time or size
  • synchronization: every two minutes, this service attempts to upload bag files with rclone
  • daily-rotation: restarts recording at midnight so bags are grouped in clean, timestamped sets
  • auto-clean: deletes local files older than 10 minutes, so the disk does not fill up with old bags. Bags live locally only as a short staging buffer

The design was built with safety in mind: recording only starts once auto-clean is running, and the sync service retries automatically. If the server is briefly unreachable, the robot retries the upload automatically.

A server setup for every team

The server itself can live wherever it makes sense for you: a machine on the local network, right where the robots operate, a self-hosted server back at your office, or simply a cloud server.

The upload side is plain rclone, which supports more than 40 storage backends. The snap always uploads to an rclone remote called bagstore independently of the configure backend. Switching from a lab server to AWS S3 is a configuration change away.

You can find below two examples of rclone configurations for the ros2-exporter-agent.

A simple SSH-accessible server (SFTP backend):

[fileserver]
type = sftp
host = bags.robot-company.com
user = robot
port = 22
key_file = /root/snap/ros2-exporter-agent/common/device_rsa_key

[bagstore]
type = alias
remote = fileserver:/srv/bags/robot-01

An S3-compatible bucket (AWS, Ceph, MinIO…):

[s3store]
type = s3
provider = Ceph
access_key_id = <access-key>
secret_access_key = <secret-key>
endpoint = https://s3.robot-company.com

[bagstore]
type = alias

Notice the pattern: the first section is backend-specific, but the bagstore alias never changes. Whether you manage one robot or a hundred with SSH or S3, the snap logic stays identical.

Set up a robot in a few minutes

Getting started takes one command and two configuration files:

sudo snap install ros2-exporter-agent --channel latest/candidate

On installation, the snap creates two templates in /var/snap/ros2-exporter-agent/common/local-configuration/.

Rename them to remove the .template suffix, then edit them:

  • rclone.conf describes where bags go using any of the backends above
  • rosbag2-recorder.yaml describes what to record, which topics to include or exclude, and how often to split bag files

The configuration section of the snap’s README documents both formats with examples.

Once both files are in place, the services pick them up and the robot starts recording and uploading on its own.

Central configuration for a fleet

Editing files on each robot works up to a certain point. However,  the snap also offers options for  managing fleets. In this case, the snap also reads its configuration through a content interface. A separate configuration snap holds rclone.conf and rosbag2-recorder.yaml, and any robot that connects to it gets the same setup. This automates away much of the manual editing. 

The rob-cos-demo-configuration repository is a ready-made example, with a ‘basic‘ branch (SFTP file server) and an ‘advanced‘ branch (S3-compatible storage).

The configuration snap also integrates some automations, such as generating a UID per device and applying the UID to the configuration. Such automations could inspire you for your own fleet.

Fork it, adapt the configuration to your own server details, build your own configuration snap, and every robot that plugs in is configured identically. By updating the configuration once, the whole fleet will receive the update.

Ideas to take it further

Once you start saving bags from your fleet, you might want to take it further with additional integrations:

  • Pull a bag to your laptop: use a small wrapper around rclone copy (or a shared alias/script) so any engineer can grab yesterday’s bag from robot-07 with one command.
  • Browse bags in a web viewer: place a lightweight file browser in front of the storage, so anyone can find and download bags from a browser.
  • Open bags straight from storage: tools like Foxglove can load a remote MCAP file by URL, so you can start inspecting a bag without downloading it first.

Further reading

  • Bring zenoh to ROS 2 with snaps
  • ROS Noetic is EoL, take actions to maintain fleet security
  • ROS development on Linux, Windows and MacOS

item.title: Fixes available for CVE-2026-98432
item.description: Fixes for the CVE-2026-98432 Linux kernel vulnerability are available for Ubuntu.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

This blog post has been updated on 9 November 2026 to reflect changes in the status of fixes for  CVE-2026-98432, a flaw in how the Linux kernel sets up IPv4 TCP connections, present in Linux kernel versions 4.4 and later.

The vulnerability has a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8, corresponding to a severity of Critical. 

Fixes for CVE-2026-98432 for Ubuntu 22.04 LTS and newer are now available in the Ubuntu archive. Our team is currently working on testing the fixes for CVE-2026-98432 for Ubuntu 20.04 LTS and older, releases under ESM support.

An earlier version of this blog post described the instructions to enable for -proposed pocket for Ubuntu archive, as the standard support fixes for CVE-2026-98432 had not completed kernel certification, our extended qualification process. This is no longer necessary.

To ensure stability across a wide ecosystem we perform extensive tests on more than 2,000 certified servers and devices. We will release the fixes for Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, 18.04 LTS and 16.04 LTS in the ESM archive for Ubuntu Pro users as soon as those tests are complete, and will update this blog with further details. Users can also check our CVE status page for up-to-date information.

Which Ubuntu releases are affected by CVE-2026-98432?

How to check if you are impacted by CVE-2026-98432

On your system, run the following command to get the version of the currently running kernel and compare the listed version to the corresponding table above.

uname -r

The list of installed kernel packages can be obtained using the following command:

dpkg -l 'linux-image*' | grep ^ii

Impact of CVE-2026-98432

The vulnerability affects the IPv4 TCP connection handling in the Linux kernel and can lead to remote code execution. The yet-unreleased exploit generated by Anthropic is described as using Multipath TCP (MPTCP), although the vulnerability is not specific to MPTCP. At the time of writing, no other exploit is known to have been generated or published.

How to apply fixes for CVE-2026-98432

We recommend you upgrade all packages:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

If this is not possible and the Linux kernel is installed via a meta package, its update can be targeted directly: 

sudo apt update
dpkg-query -W -f '${source:Package}\t${binary:Package}\n' | awk '$1 ~ "^linux-meta" { print $2 }' | xargs sudo apt install --only-upgrade

Once the security updates for the Linux kernel are installed, a reboot is required:

sudo reboot

Ubuntu 26.10, 26.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, and 22.04 LTS receive these fixes as part of standard support. 

If you are using Ubuntu 20.04 LTS or older, the Ubuntu Pro subscription offers coverage for up to 15 years. Ubuntu 20.04 LTS and 18.04 LTS are covered by Expanded Security Maintenance (ESM), while Ubuntu 16.04 LTS and 14.04 LTS require ESM with the Legacy add-on. Ubuntu Pro is free for up to 5 machines, or up to 50 machines for community members. Ubuntu Pro also provides access to Landscape which enables you to control the roll-out of security fixes across your estate. Learn more.

Mitigations for CVE-2026-98432

Mitigations that disable multipath TCP (MPTCP) are being recommended by various sources, but please note that the CVE fix is not specific to MPTCP. The recommendations are based exclusively on the fact that the yet-unreleased exploit generated by Anthropic is described as using MPTCP; no other exploit is known to have been generated or published. The Ubuntu Security Team believes that security updates are the only appropriate mitigation. For Ubuntu 22.04 LTS and newer, these are currently in qualification testing and available in the -proposed pocket, as mentioned above. 

Managing the -proposed pocket

A previous version of this blog referenced  instructions to enable the -proposed pocket, as standard support release updates were undergoing kernel certification, our extended qualification process. This is no longer necessary for CVE-2026-98432, as the fixes are available in the -updates pocket of the Ubuntu archive. You can retain the configuration of the -proposed pocket and have early access to kernel security updates for subsequent cycles.

We recommended the following command to enable the -proposed pocket:

sudo add-apt-repository --component main --pocket proposed http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu

To disable the -proposed pocket after it had previously been enabled, use the following command:

sudo add-apt-repository --remove --component main --pocket proposed http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu

On Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, enabling the -proposed pocket can result in unintended upgrades being applied, because the -proposed pocket is used for Stable Release Updates (SRUs) for all userspace packages, as well. You can lower the priority of the -proposed pocket by using the following command:

cat << 'EOF' | sudo tee /etc/apt/preferences.d/proposed
Package: *
Pin: release a=jammy-proposed
Pin-Priority: 400
EOF 

On Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and newer, packages from the -proposed pocket are not selected for upgrade by default. You have to explicitly install the package by specifying the -proposed pocket corresponding to your release. For example, if your kernel has been installed via a meta-package, you can use the following command:

sudo apt update
dpkg-query -W -f '${source:Package}\t${binary:Package}\n' | awk '$1 ~ "^linux-meta" { print $2 }' | xargs sudo apt install -t $(. /etc/os-release && echo $VERSION_CODENAME)-proposed --only-upgrade

References

  • https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-98432
  • https://www.anthropic.com/research/discovering-vulnerabilities-with-claude

item.content:encoded:
Introduction


Two critical security vulnerabilities affecting PHP have been identified that result in unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) for any PHP application. The vulnerabilities have been assigned the CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 identifiers, but are also referred to using the php2shell nickname. Ubuntu has released fixes for the affected packages for all supported releases.

The two vulnerabilities both have a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, corresponding to a severity of CRITICAL.

The vulnerabilities have been responsibly disclosed and the PHP Foundation has engaged in coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) with distributors, establishing a public disclosure date of 22 October 2026 at 14:00 UTC. However, due to a public leak, the disclosure date has been moved forward to 21 October 2026 14:00 UTC.

Which Ubuntu releases are affected by php2shell?

How to check if you are impacted by php2shell

You can verify the versions of any packages installed matching the PHP interpreter package name with the following command:

apt list '?installed ?name(^php[0-9.]+$)'

Impact of php2shell

The two vulnerabilities affect any PHP application. An unauthenticated attacker with network access to the web application can trivially achieve arbitrary remote code execution with the PHP application’s credentials on the target system.

How to apply fixes for php2shell

We recommend you upgrade all packages:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

If this is not possible, the affected component can be targeted:

sudo apt update && sudo apt install --only-upgrade '?name(^php[0-9.]+$)'

The application that uses the PHP interpreter would likely need to be restarted. For example, for an application using apache2 with mod_php, restarting the apache daemon is required:

sudo systemctl restart apache2

Alternatively, the system can be rebooted to ensure that all applications use the updated components:

sudo reboot

The unattended-upgrades feature is enabled by default for Ubuntu 16.04 LTS onwards. This feature:  

  • Applies new security updates every 24 hours automatically.
  • If you have this enabled, the patches above will be automatically applied within 24 hours of being available, but the affected applications would still need to be restarted or the system rebooted.

Ubuntu 26.10, 26.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, and 22.04 LTS receive these fixes as part of standard support. If you are using Ubuntu 20.04 LTS or older, the Ubuntu Pro subscription offers coverage for up to 15 years. Ubuntu 20.04 LTS and 18.04 LTS are covered by Expanded Security Maintenance (ESM), while Ubuntu 16.04 LTS and 14.04 LTS require ESM with the Legacy add-on. Ubuntu Pro is free for up to 5 machines, or up to 50 machines for community members. Ubuntu Pro also provides access to Landscape which enables you to control the roll-out of security fixes across your estate. Learn more.

  • https://ubuntu.com/security/notices/USN-8948-2
  • https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-21-5

item.content:encoded:
This blog post was updated with additional information related to libnss3 and Java applications on October 22, 2026. For more information on Ubuntu Core fixes, you can also check our Discourse post.

Introduction

The private keys of the eMudhra Certificate Authority (CA) have been demonstrated on 20 October 2026 to have been compromised. The Ubuntu Security Team has released updates to the system PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) root CA store in the ca-certificates package, as well as in the libnss3 library.

On 21 October, Oracle issued CVE-2026-91403 to address the same issue for users of Oracle Java. OpenJDK distributed by Ubuntu is not affected, as it is modified to use the system root CA store. However, due to an unrelated issue, the Java root CA store requires manual action as detailed below to ensure synchronization.

While the eMudhra CA is not directly trusted as a root on Ubuntu, two other root CAs have cross-signed the eMudhra CA: emSign Root TLS CA – G3 and Comodo AAA Certificate Services. These two roots have been removed from the Ubuntu trusted root stores to ensure that the compromised eMudhra CA is no longer trusted. Any legitimate certificate which is ultimately trusted by either of these two root CAs would no longer be trusted. It is unlikely, but this may result in some hosts being unreachable, due to their use of the revoked certificate. The AAA Certificate Services CA had previously been removed from the CA bundles in Ubuntu 22.04 (Jammy Jellyfish) and newer releases.

Which Ubuntu releases are affected?

ReleasePackage NameRemediation status
Trusty (14.04)ca-certificatesFixed in 20230311~14.04.1~esm3
Xenial (16.04)ca-certificatesFixed in 202402031~16.04.1~esm3
Bionic (18.04)ca-certificatesFixed in 202402031ubuntu0.18.04.1+esm3
Focal (20.04)ca-certificatesFixed in 20240203~20.04.1ubuntu0.1~esm2
Jammy (22.04)ca-certificatesFixed in 20260816ubuntu0.22.04.1
Noble (24.04)ca-certificatesFixed in 20260816ubuntu0.24.04.1
Resolute (26.04)ca-certificatesFixed in 20260816ubuntu0.26.04.1
Stonking (26.10)ca-certificatesFixed in 20260816ubuntu0.26.10.1

How to check if you are impacted

You can verify the version of the affected packages with the following command:

dpkg -l ca-certificates 'libnss3*' | grep ^ii

Users of Java applications need to apply a manual mitigation, detailed in the ‘Updating the Java root CA store’ section below.

Desktop users should take special notice of their browsers installed as snap packages and follow the recommendation in the ‘Note for Ubuntu Desktop users’ section below.

Impact of the CA Compromise

An unauthorized third party would be able to sign fraudulent X.509 certificates; these would pass validation by a TLS implementation (commonly TLS clients) that trusts the eMudhra CA. Mitigations such as public key pinning or DNS Certificate Authority Authorization (CAA) records do provide the ability to detect such fraudulent certificates, but depend on the TLS application making use of the mitigations and are not widely used.

This could lead to the identity impersonation of a TLS endpoint and could allow an attacker-in-the-middle to intercept and compromise the confidentiality and integrity of TLS connections, irrespective of the CA that the authentic TLS endpoint uses, unless mitigations are employed.

How to apply fixes

We recommend you upgrade all packages:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

If this is not possible, the affected component can be targeted:

sudo apt update && sudo apt install --only-upgrade ca-certificates 'libnss3*'

The unattended-upgrades feature is enabled by default for Ubuntu 16.04 LTS onwards. This feature:  

  • Applies new security updates every 24 hours automatically.
  • If you have this enabled, the patches above will be automatically applied within 24 hours of being available.

Ubuntu 26.10, 26.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, and 22.04 LTS receive these fixes as part of standard support. If you are using Ubuntu 20.04 LTS or older, you can apply this fix with an Ubuntu Pro subscription via the Expanded Security Maintenance (ESM) service. Ubuntu Pro is free for up to 5 machines, or up to 50 machines for community members. Ubuntu Pro also provides access to Landscape which enables you to control the roll-out of security fixes across your estate. Learn more. 

Updating the Java root CA store

The instructions in this section are only necessary if you use any Java applications.

The Java root CA store is normally synchronized from the ca-certificates package containing the system root CA store. However, this synchronization is currently affected by an unresolved issue. This means that at present, removing the compromised certificates requires additional manual action after the ca-certificates package has been updated according to the section above.

If the Java root CA store contains locally-provisioned CA certificates that are not part of the system root CA store, these will need to be re-added after the following commands are executed.

First, delete the existing Java root CA store:

sudo rm -f /etc/ssl/certs/java/cacerts

Then, regenerate the Java root CA store from the system CA store:

sudo update-ca-certificates --fresh

Note for Ubuntu Desktop users

On Ubuntu Desktop, the most common TLS client would be a browser. They are typically installed as snap packages on Ubuntu desktop, and do not use the system trust store provided by the ca-certificates package. Snap packages are refreshed four times a day by default. If you have disabled automatic updates, ensure that you refresh your snaps manually.

References

  • https://ubuntu.com/security/notices/USN-8944-1
  • https://ubuntu.com/security/notices/USN-8944-2
  • https://ubuntu.com/security/notices/USN-8947-1
  • https://emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/
  • https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/alert-cve-2026-91403.html

item.title: How to lower Android™ development costs by removing hardware from the critical path
item.description: As an Android developer, you’ll almost always have access to a device. item.content:encoded:
As an Android developer, you’ll almost always have access to a device. However, when handling hardware, the device that you actually need often happens to be already in use, set up incorrectly, stored in another lab, or simply waiting to be reset. That’s when Android development costs start to increase.

Because it’s not just the device itself that generates expenses, it’s everything around it: procurement, provisioning, maintenance, remote access, lab capacity, and, worst of all: your engineering time. A developer waiting for the right dev environment still constitutes a cost.

So, how can you solve that problem?

Do my tests actually need hardware?

We all know that hardware still plays a big role in Android development. If you need to validate sensors, peripherals, real target performance, the hardware integration itself, or even the genuine user experience, you’re going to need the physical target device.

But most workloads competing for those devices can run elsewhere.

When building Android, testing an application, reproducing a bug, or even running regression tests, there’s absolutely no need for any physical device. So instead of asking yourself if a specific target device is available, the question you should ask is whether you need a device at all.

The distinction is important here, because hardware labs are obviously much harder to scale than software.

More developers often means more builds, more tests, and more configurations. That typically means a higher need for devices, benches, and more infrastructure to have enough capacity for peak times when relying on hardware-first. As you can see, Android development costs aren’t only a result of the gear itself, but the effort to run it, and the engineering time lost when access becomes a bottleneck.

Android infrastructure operations

When moving workloads away from hardware, Android environments can then be provisioned when needed, integrated into Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery/Deployment (CI/CD) pipelines, run in parallel, and discarded afterwards. A cloud-first approach is much simpler than a hardware one. Just request your environment, run your tests, and safely release it.

The secret trick is to be wise when choosing the appropriate execution environment for the job you want to run: use containers when you need app density and scale, virtual machines if you need to run a custom Android image, and physical devices for when the tests truly depend on physical components.

With Anbox Cloud, these cloud environments can co-exist in exactly the same development workflow. Developers can continue using familiar tools such as Android Debug Bridge (ADB), Android Studio, their existing test frameworks, and usual CI/CD systems.

Let’s take the example of a support or validation team that needs to reproduce issues across many Android configurations. In a hardware-first setup, that means finding the right device, checking its software version, reserving it, reconfiguring it, and setting up remote access before debugging even starts.

With cloud-based Android environments, the same team can keep predefined images for common configurations and start them on demand. Several engineers can work in parallel, while physical devices are reserved for cases that truly require hardware validation.

In this instance, costs are lowered not simply because there is one less phone on a shelf. It is the time spent finding, preparing, and sharing that phone and the extra capacity required to make sure one is available when demand peaks. A device sitting idle is inefficient. An engineer sitting idle because the right device isn’t available is even more expensive.

Where Android development costs actually come from, and how to reduce your expenses

Generally, there are three cost areas worth looking at: the first obvious cost is hardware, then operations (setup, maintenance, and so on), and, last but not least: engineering time. The impact of that last element is easy to underestimate.

If fewer workloads depend on dedicated devices, teams need less hardware capacity to support the same level of development activity. Here is how using Anbox Cloud helps you to improve these three cost areas:

  • Hardware cost: fewer devices, benches, and supporting infrastructure need to be provisioned for peak demand
  • Operational cost: less manual setup, maintenance, and environment management
  • Engineering-time cost: less waiting for shared resources and more opportunities to run workloads in parallel

If ten tests need to run, they should not necessarily queue behind the same physical bench. If an issue needs to be reproduced, an engineer should not have to spend time rebuilding the right configuration manually. Software-defined environments can be created specifically for the workload and removed afterwards.

That also means that the customized hardware you do have can then be reserved for the tests that can’t do without it. Reducing Android development cost therefore becomes more than reducing hardware spending. It becomes a way to get more engineering work from the infrastructure, as well as getting back the engineering time you already have.

Take hardware out of the critical path

As I like to say, the point here is not to completely get rid of physical devices. The goal is to make sure to only use your expensive hardware because the test requires it, not because the workflow was built around it.

That means running software-driven workloads early, running more of them in parallel, and keeping those physical benches for the validation or certification work where they provide actual value.

Instead of scaling Android development by continuously adding devices, scale the environments around them. Less wait, more scaling, faster iterations.

Stop running after devices. Run Android in the cloud.

item.content:encoded:
The latest interim release of Ubuntu previews privacy conscious speech-to-text, enables post-quantum package signing, completes the rollout of Rust coreutils, and improves enterprise identity integration.

October 15, 2026

Today Canonical announced the release of Ubuntu 26.10, codenamed “Stonking Stingray,” available to download and install from ubuntu.com/download. 

Building on previous releases, Ubuntu 26.10 advances enterprise security features, completes the rollout of the Rust-based uutils coreutils, and strengthens integrations for user authentication using Microsoft Entra ID. Ubuntu 26.10 also introduces post-quantum package signing, demonstrating that interim releases both build on established ground, and look towards the future.

Earlier this year, we set out a roadmap for AI on Ubuntu. Stonking Stingray delivers the first milestone through the integration of Myna: a speech-to-text agent that utilizes on-device LLMs. We’ve led Ubuntu’s first AI integration with accessibility to ensure that cutting-edge features are available to all users from day one.

Users will also benefit from enhanced security features. Ubuntu 26.10 completes the migration to Rust-based coreutils, and broadens device support for TPM-backed FDE.  Stonking Stingray is symbolic of Ubuntu’s journey to not just build up, but also build out.

Jon Seager, VP of Ubuntu Engineering at Canonical
Download Ubuntu 26.10 for free Register for Ubuntu Summit 26.10 ›

Elegance and accessibility with new speech-to-text agent

Stonking Stingray brings us the debut of Myna: Ubuntu’s speech-to-text agent. Named after the Myna bird (known for its ability to mimic human speech),  Myna is an opt-in feature in Ubuntu 26.10, designed to provide speech recognition with clear visual feedback while you speak. Based on local models, Myna offers speech-to-text, without sacrificing privacy. Myna will continue to evolve and as Ubuntu 28.04 LTS approaches, it will be included by default with Ubuntu.

Myna marks the first step towards a more natural, intent-driven Ubuntu Desktop experience that will enable users to express what they want to achieve, rather than manually navigate applications and settings. For example, a developer could simply say, “Help me investigate why my tests are failing,” and Ubuntu could analyze test results, locate relevant code, and prepare a workspace with the tools and information needed to troubleshoot the issue. 

Ubuntu 26.10 also ships with GNOME 51, bringing a smoother, more responsive desktop, better display handling, improved accessibility, and refinements across core applications. In addition, the Ubuntu App Center now provides a more consistent experience for managing snaps and debs.

Users of assistive technology will benefit from improved support for Flutter applications, with assistive technologies like Orca (screen-reader) now able to better parse and understand the content included in Flutter applications.

This release also brings reliability enhancements to the desktop userspace layers. Ubuntu 26.10 adopts dbus-broker as the default D-Bus implementation, replacing legacy message queuing between apps with strict per-app message accounting, ensuring a single app can’t stall the desktop. Additionally, desktop OOM (out-of-memory protection) scoring has been adjusted to better manage–memory pressure in userspace.

Security for present and future threats

Ubuntu Desktop now integrates more naturally with Microsoft identity services, including password with Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), and passwordless authentication. This ensures devices can authenticate securely by default,  and under the same security umbrella as Windows devices in the same organization.

TPM-backed full-disk encryption, which was rolled out in Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, has been expanded to encompass hardware models lacking a Hardware Root of Trust, with users being able to require a PIN or passphrase. These features ensure that users can use Ubuntu with best practice security enabled by default. 

Ubuntu 26.10 delivers post-quantum ready package signing, by replacing GnuPG with Sequoia PGP to verify APT repository signatures. Sequoia brings Rust’s memory-safe practices to package signing and acts as a barrier to the threat of quantum cryptographic attack attempts. Ubuntu 26.10 introduces quantum-safe token support via openCryptoki, providing robust PKCS #11 V3.2 coverage across multiple token types, including Soft, EP11, and CCA tokens with ML-DSA and ML-KEM integration.

A new kernel. The latest hardware. 

Ubuntu 26.10 brings Linux kernel 7.3, which facilitates hardware enablement for the latest silicon, such as Intel Xe3P (Nova Lake), AMD Zen 6, and NVIDIA 615. As heterogeneous platforms like these span CPU cores, GPUs, and media decoders, the latest kernel brings the direct rendering management and power management hooks needed for these components to perform. 

Kernel 7.3 also enhances the way data is handled at the software level, through out-of-the-box support for Lustre, a parallel distributed file system designed to transfer massive datasets simultaneously across thousands of corporate nodes. 

Ubuntu 26.10 continues the tradition of delivering architecture-focused enhancements. Stonking Stingray will launch with a dedicated installer for amd64v3 hardware, ensuring that users with modern platforms get an optimized experience. For RISC-V users, Ubuntu 26.10 brings desktop images, complementing the work that had already been done to do so with Server images. This includes support for the first RVA23-enabled RISC-V hardware, the SpacemiT K3, ensuring that developers can meet the new standard with confidence on a stable OS. Together, these enhancements streamline setup for developers building on cutting-edge silicon.

item.content:encoded:
Introduction

On 7 October 2026, Daniel Stenberg published a blog post describing a plan to release a new version of curl on 14 October 2026 in order to address 22 known security vulnerabilities. These vulnerabilities have varying severities, with a single vulnerability assessed as high (CVE-2026-92392), while the others have a low or medium severity. The curl maintainer has coordinated with downstream vendors, including Ubuntu, under embargo and the vulnerabilities have been publicly disclosed on the planned date. All operating systems that distribute curl are affected, including Linux distributions. Ubuntu has released updates that address all vulnerabilities for all affected releases: USN-8927-1 and USN-8932-1. CVE-2026-92392 only impacts Ubuntu 26.04 LTS (Resolute Raccoon).

The vulnerabilities do not have CVSS scores assigned. CVE-2026-92392 was assessed by the Ubuntu Security Team to have a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1, corresponding to a severity of HIGH (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H).

The vulnerabilities affect both the curl command-line utility and the libcurl library. The following are the identifiers associated with the vulnerabilities:

  • CVE-2026-107929
  • CVE-2026-107928
  • CVE-2026-94266

Which Ubuntu releases are affected?

How to check if you are impacted

You can verify the versions of any packages installed from the curl source package with the following command.

apt list '?installed ?source-package(^curl$)'

Impact of CVE-2026-92392

CVE-2026-92392 is known to allow remote code execution. Successful exploitation requires a malicious server, so this issue can be mitigated by only contacting trusted servers. The conditions required to reach and exploit this issue are complex.

Impact of the other vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-92388 is also a use-after-free vulnerability, the same class as CVE-2026-92392. This class of vulnerabilities is typically considered to lead to remote code execution in conservative assessments. However, CVE-2026-92388 does not affect the curl command-line utility and is only applicable if an application using the libcurl library uses the FTP functionality in a certain way. The vulnerability has therefore been assessed by the curl project with a low severity.

The other CVEs include leaking authentication credentials to incorrect connections through a variety of protocols and proxies (including Kerberos tickets); protocol state machine problems with TFTP and IMAP that could lead to denial-of-service or information disclosure issues; HTTP servers able to wipe or truncate cookie jars; HSTS expiration and durability issues; SSH host key checking issues; a data leak in the GnuTLS version; memory exhaustion leading to denial-of-service; two issues for TLS backends we do not support.

How to apply fixes

We recommend you upgrade all packages:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

If this is not possible, the affected component can be targeted:

sudo apt update && sudo apt install --only-upgrade '?source-package(^curl$)'

The unattended-upgrades feature is enabled by default for Ubuntu 16.04 LTS onwards. This service:  

  • Applies new security updates every 24 hours automatically.
  • If you have this enabled, the patches above will be automatically applied within 24 hours of being available.

Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, and 22.04 LTS receive these fixes as part of standard support. If you are using Ubuntu 20.04 LTS or older, you can apply this fix with an Ubuntu Pro subscription via the Expanded Security Maintenance (ESM) service. Ubuntu Pro is free for up to 5 machines, or up to 50 machines for community members. Ubuntu Pro also provides access to Landscape which enables you to control the roll-out of security fixes across your estate.

item.content:encoded:
A few months ago, we introduced Myna, our project to bring private, local speech-to-text dictation to Ubuntu Desktop. Named after the speech-mimicking myna bird, Myna is an optional Ubuntu 26.10 feature that offers real-time visual feedback during speech recognition.

Since then, Myna has grown into something you can install and use on your desktop.

Today, we’re making it available as a technology preview to the wider Ubuntu community. Whether you regularly rely upon speech-to-text dictation, or only use it for certain use cases, we want to hear your feedback.

Myna is still under active development, so you should expect some rough edges. The core experience is there: press a shortcut, speak, and Myna transcribes directly into the application you’re using.

Local speech-to-text

Speech recognition runs entirely on your machine. Once a model has been downloaded, no internet connection is required for transcription, and your audio is not uploaded or stored.

Myna supports several speech recognition engines, including Parakeet, Whisper, and FunASR, each with different trade-offs in language support, accuracy, and hardware requirements.

Trying Myna

Myna is currently available on Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, and Ubuntu 26.10, on amd64 and amd64v3, using GNOME on Wayland.

To install the preview, run:

sudo add-apt-repository ppa:canonical-desktop-team/myna
sudo apt install myna-config

Then open Myna settings from Activities and follow the setup.

If you have a supported NVIDIA GPU, Myna can also offer a GPU-accelerated engine. Support for additional accelerators is planned.

Once setup is complete, put the cursor in a text field, press the configured hotkey, and start talking.

What we’d like you to try

Use Myna with the applications you normally use, in your native language or any language with your natural accent.

We’re particularly interested in feedback on:

  • Transcription quality
  • Responsiveness
  • Language and accent support
  • Application compatibility
  • Setup and onboarding
  • Anything that feels awkward or unexpected

Different machines and microphones are useful too, as we want to understand how well the current models and defaults behave across a broad range of Ubuntu systems.

For now, Myna is deliberately focused on dictation. It is not a voice assistant and does not control the desktop through voice commands.

Get involved

Myna is developed in the open at github.com/canonical/myna.

You can:

  • Report bugs on GitHub
  • Start or join discussions
  • Contribute code, documentation, or ideas

If speech-to-text is something you rely on, we’re especially interested in hearing about your experience and what is still missing.

Thanks to everyone who has already tested Myna and shared feedback with us.

item.title: [$] Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
item.dc:creator: jzb
item.description: Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms.

item.dc:creator: corbet
item.description: One of the dominant themes of 2026 has been the debate within development projects about the terms under which LLM-written contributions should be accepted — if, indeed, they should be accepted at all. Linus Torvalds has released the 7.4-rc2 prepatch and it will come as no surprise that it is a large one ("a big -rc2 to go with the largest ever -rc1"). Much of the size was made up of some automated Coccinelle updates that were spread out all over the tree; once those are factored out, the rest looks fairly normal:
When masking that noise out from the diffstat, the shape of it changes - not spread out over thousands of files any more. But it does not look unusual: a third is drivers (gpu, networking and sound account for most of it, but there's a bit of everything), another third is networking and bpf, and the final third is "the rest" (mostly filesystems, mm, arch updates).

And yes, much of this was driven by various AI fixes. I think I'll stop repeating that, and we can just take it for granted. But this time around Alexei [Starovoitov] claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true.

item.title: Asahi Linux 7.3 progress report
item.dc:creator: corbet
item.description:
The Asahi Linux developers have put out a new report on their progress toward a Linux distribution for Apple devices.

Some time ago, we were made aware of multiple attempts to exploit our permissive licensing to hijack our work, with a direct view to replacing the project and aggressively monetising Linux on Apple Silicon. In some extreme cases, in-development feature code was being lifted straight out of our personal forks and published without attribution or lazily rewritten with LLM assistance to obfuscate its origin. The MIT licence explicitly allows this, and has no carveouts to protect against bad faith actors.

As such, we made the difficult decision to begin the process of transitioning all of our repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. Going forward all Asahi Linux code will be licenced under strong copyleft licences only. Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it.

Lennart Poettering, Michael Vogt, and Joaquim Rocha have put together a detailed overview of what the Amutable Operating System (AOS) and associated infrastructure will look like.

item.title: [$] Locking down hibernation for the winter
item.dc:creator: daroc
item.description: When a computer hibernates, the kernel writes the contents of memory to disk and then shuts the system down. Resuming from hibernation involves reading that data back into memory, and then having the kernel pick up where it left off. Unfortunately, the kernel does not have any way to know that the data it is reading back has not been tampered with, which is why lockdown, an optional kernel feature that attempts to prevent modifications to the running kernel, disables hibernation. Matthew Garrett, who has been working on lockdown for many years, has shared a patch set that aims to fix this problem. His solution must also protect against downgrade attacks (where an attacker reboots the computer with an older kernel version to bypass new protections), which complicates the implementation.
